research_concepts: play-type label construction and quality from play-by-play
methodological_questions: Is the opponent T+1 PPP shift after a play type large enough, relative to direct PPP gaps, to change an AVOID label?
Do own-sequence lags survive within-team, score-state and opponent controls, and do they decay with lag?
Are play-type labels accurate enough (foul leakage, assisted-flag leakage, OTHER share) to support play-level contrasts?
How is multiplicity handled across play types, lags and players?

historical_evidence.finding: Extended possession value: 4 of 8 play types showed a real downstream (opponent T+1) component (CUT +0.0220, TRANSITION +0.0145, SPOT_UP +0.0124, POST_UP +0.0194 PPP suppression). DRIVE downstream was not real (+0.0024). Recorded failure evidence: downstream effects are small (~0.01-0.02 PPP) relative to direct PPP gaps. Player-level downstream effects were mostly non-findings after BH correction.

Persistent Impact Score Level 1 gate FAILED the decay sanity check. DRIVE lag lifts were flat (+0.015 to +0.021 across lags) and collapsed within team (lag-1 +0.015 to -0.002). Cohen d was about 0.01-0.03 with p~0 from n>150k, on 915,570 possessions. Callable play-type horizons = 0. Recorded cause: team-quality confound.

After the opponent runs play type X, the next offensive play type scores above baseline. Defensive aftershock of about +0.12 to +0.135 PPP replicated in 8/8 play types, in all games and in playoffs. Limited by small samples in some pair cells. The records returned do not show whether it was controlled for team quality or possession-ending type.
Star-level sequential suppression (PUTBACK as top suppressor) with n_after of 32-95 in several cells, no multiplicity correction, and a drift risk. Not an adequately powered test.
Labeling audit: OTHER has 36% foul endings, which inflates its PPP. DRIVE sits 12pp below the foul benchmark (FOUL_LEAK). initiation_type maps only 0.7% of 50,668 possessions.
The assisted flag exists only on makes, which produced SPOT_UP 2.83 PPP and TRANSITION 0.62 PPP. After a rewrite they were about 1.16 and 1.20.
Label audit FAILED: OTHER 20.2% vs a <10% target, 40.8% low confidence, DRIVE foul-draw 1.7% vs a 14-22% benchmark. Described as systematic label issues that undermine findings.
Backfill verification FAILED: PNR share too high, PULL_UP about 0-2% for many teams in 2024-25, 82.8% of PNR labels proxy_calibrated, team identity checks failed.
Defensive scheme labeling (DROP/ICE/SWITCH) reached only 3-15% confident labels, and switches_on was unpopulated. This bears on coverage-based explanations of T+1 effects.
Holdout games with a play-type mix closer to the model's recommended mix scored better (+3.27 ORtg strength-controlled; n=908 rows, no CI, same-pipeline validation). Relevant only indirectly.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Treating cross-possession lag lifts as play-type memory (lag-1 >= lag-2)
failed_approaches.why: Lifts were flat across lags and collapsed under within-team baselines, which indicates a team-quality confound. Huge n gave p~0 with tiny effect sizes.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Play-type PPP from a classifier that used an outcome-dependent assisted flag
failed_approaches.why: Construction artifact: the flag exists only on makes, so SPOT_UP PPP was inflated to 2.83.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Comparing play-type PPP without accounting for foul endings
failed_approaches.why: Foul-bucket and foul-leak artifacts inflated OTHER and deflated DRIVE.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Using the inferred labels as reliable inputs for adaptation findings
failed_approaches.why: The audit failed on distribution, foul rates, PPP bands and team identities.
Label error: PULL_UP near 0 for many 2024-25 teams, PNR over-assigned, mostly proxy-calibrated labels.
Small cells (n_after 32-95) and no multiplicity correction.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Labeling defensive scheme from NBA matchup/PBP fields
failed_approaches.why: Label rates were too low and switches_on was not populated.

evidence_establishes: Per FAM:SF-APPS-075, measured opponent T+1 effects for the play types it examined are small (about 0.01-0.02 PPP), smaller than direct PPP gaps, and absent for DRIVE.
Per FAM:SF-CHT-029, own-sequence lag effects did not show decay and collapsed within team, so no callable play-type horizon exists. This was recorded as an artifact of team-quality confounding.

Per FAM:SF-CHT-025, FAM:SF-PAP-096, FAM:SF-APPM-014 and FAM:SF-APPA-030, the play-type labels have had construction, foul-leakage and distributional defects. Differences in PPP by play type can be artifacts.
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether a specific, pre-defined AVOID rule would flip for any play type once T+1 effects are included. The AVOID threshold is not defined in the retrieved records.
Whether the larger SF07 aftershock (+0.12 PPP) reflects genuine causal downstream effects. The returned text does not show controls for possession-ending type, team quality or score state.
Whether the T+1 effects in FAM:SF-APPS-075 survive after the label fixes and correct handling of the ending type of the preceding possession. The record gives no controls, validation or CI.
Whether results hold on 2025-26 data. The retrieved records do not say which seasons they used.
Any causal interpretation. All records are observational.
own_inferences: Opponent T+1 PPP after your play depends mechanically on how your possession ended (made shot -> opponent half-court; miss/turnover -> transition). So an unconditional T+1 comparison confounds play type with ending type and is a likely source of the large SF07 aftershock.

Even a real 0.01-0.02 PPP T+1 shift is likely too small to change an AVOID label, unless the play type's direct PPP sits within about 0.02 of the threshold. The question's premise (large enough to drive AVOID) is therefore more likely to be rejected than supported.
The question can be answered more cleanly as a magnitude test (does T+1 change an AVOID classification?) than as an existence test, because with n>100k almost any effect gets p~0.
Own-sequence lags are likely to show up as team-quality, pace and score-state effects, as FAM:SF-CHT-029 did, unless estimated within team-season and by game.
uncertainties: The AVOID label definition and threshold are not provided or retrieved.
The retrieved records were truncated and I did not read the full text of SF07 or SF-APPS-075 for methods and controls.
The current state of the label pipeline after the earlier audits is unknown.
The 2025-26 playoffs are partial on the question date (complete from 2026-06-21), so that sample should not be used as a holdout until complete.

historical_effect.explanation: Without the history, the question could be run as a direct test on the inferred play-type labels. The history shows that T+1 effects are small relative to direct gaps, lag effects collapse within team, and the labels have repeatedly produced artifacts. So I recommend a narrowed, label-gated test with within-team baselines and ending-type conditioning, and I lower the chance that the premise is supported.

methodological_questions: Is opponent next-possession PPP after a play type large enough to drive AVOID labels?
Do own-sequence lagged play types (previous possessions) materially affect outcomes beyond the current play type?
How do selection, score state, lineup and opponent quality confound next-possession effects?
How reliable is play-type labeling derived from play-by-play, and does outcome-derived labeling bias results?
What sample size and multiple-testing control is needed across many play types?
args.query: next-possession opponent PPP after play type, AVOID label, lag effects, play-type labeling data quality

system_prompt:
You are a basketball analytics researcher deciding whether and how a research question should be studied.
You work only from the task statement and the tools listed below. Do not assume facts you have not seen.

The work has two stages, in this order.
Stage 1, retrieval:
1. Read the research objective and the data description.
2. Identify the research concepts and methodological questions the task raises.
3. Retrieve historical evidence by calling retrieve_history.
In stage 1 do not assess the question, predict outcomes or decide. Your only stage-1 reply is the retrieve_history call.
Stage 2, assessment, after the retrieval result is returned:
4. Summarise the relevant historical findings and failed approaches.
5. State what the historical evidence does and does not establish.
6. Assess whether the research question is testable.
7. Identify methodological risks and potential confounders.
8. Make the final research decision.
9. Explain whether and how the historical evidence changed the decision.
The stage-2 output format is given together with the retrieval result.

Evidence rules: keep what a retrieved record states (historical_evidence and failed_approaches, each citing the
identifier of a returned record and its status exactly as recorded) separate from your own inference and from
uncertainty or missing information. Cite only identifiers returned by a tool, and never describe an earlier study that
no tool returned. In some settings retrieval returns no records; then state that no historical evidence was available.

Tools:
- retrieve_history(research_concepts, methodological_questions, query): the prescribed retrieval step. Returns the most relevant consolidated study-family records of earlier research by this project that are available in this setting, with their identifiers; returns an empty list when none are available.
- glossary(): definitions of basketball and project terms used in task statements.
- data_catalog(): the fields available in each per-game data file.
- search_documents(query): rank further study-family documents by text relevance; returns up to 10 families not yet returned.
- read_family(id): the complete record of one study family (for example 'FAM:SF-APPA-001').

Protocol: every reply is exactly one JSON object and nothing else.
To call a tool: {"action": "tool", "tool": "<name>", "args": {...}}
To finish (stage 2 only): {"action": "final", "output": <object following the stage-2 schema>}
You may call at most 12 tools; then you must finish. Check that every opening brace has a closing brace.

Risk codes (use only these): SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, EXPOSURE_SPARSITY, MEASURE_RELIABILITY, RTM_SELECTION, OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL, LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD, MECHANICAL_FLOOR, BASE_RATE, CONFOUNDING, LABEL_ERROR, PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE, MULTIPLE_TESTING, IMPLEMENTATION_BUG, DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY

Research question (as posed on 2026-06-19, in the area of play-type labeling and data quality):
Opponent next-possession PPP after you run play X is large enough to drive AVOID labels; own-sequence lags similarly matter.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

Stage 1. Reply only with the retrieval call: {"action": "tool", "tool": "retrieve_history", "args": {"research_concepts": ["..."], "methodological_questions": ["..."], "query": "..."}}

Field guidance:
- historical_evidence and failed_approaches: only records returned by a tool, with the status as recorded; empty lists
  if nothing relevant was returned.
- testability.p_testable: probability that the question can be answered with the stated data at useful statistical power.
- prior_work.already_answered: whether retrieved earlier work already answered substantially the same question.

- predicted_outcome: probabilities (summing to 1) of what a competent test of the question as posed would conclude:
  supported, rejected (adequately powered null), untestable (cannot be tested with this data), artifact (apparent
  effect produced by a flaw), uncertain (inconclusive or inadequately tested).

reasoning_details.text:
I'm weighing whether to pull more records, but the snippets I have look sufficient, so I'm inclined to wrap up directly while staying careful about what I claim. The core question is whether the opponent's next-possession PPP after running play X is large enough to drive AVOID labels, and the APPS-075 evidence shows downstream effects of only about 0.01 to 0.02.

I'm checking the remaining evidence: the APPS-075 and CHT-029 effects look small, and the SF07 aftershock of about +0.12 probably reflects mechanical sequencing after a made basket or transition rather than a real lag. I'm also noting a handful of records that may be labeling artifacts, and that the AVOID threshold isn't defined in what I've retrieved.

Since the downstream effects are mechanical, depending on how the possession ended, I'd condition on the ending type and treat the team-quality confound separately. I'm also assigning rough probabilities to the outcomes: supported at 0.15, rejected at 0.4, untestable at 0.05, artifact at 0.2, and uncertain at 0.2, with about a 0.7 chance the question is testable at all.
